analysis.one_liner: Reclassifies broadband as a regulated common-carrier service to enable net neutrality rules.
analysis.headline: With 42 House Democratic sponsors, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Communications Act to define broadband internet as a telecommunications service rather than a lightly regulated information service. That would give the Federal Communications Commission authority to apply common-carrier rules to internet providers — the legal basis for net neutrality protections like bans on blocking, slowing down, or charging websites for faster delivery. The bill never moved past the introductory referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users, who would gain enforceable protections against broadband providers blocking websites, slowing traffic, or charging fees for priority delivery; and websites and online services that would no longer need to pay providers for better access to their own customers.

how_it_helps.text: Classifies broadband internet access service as a telecommunications service under the Communications Act, the legal category that subjects providers to common-carrier requirements [S2] [S3].
Common-carrier rules are the basis for net neutrality protections, which restrict broadband providers from blocking or throttling lawful content and from paid fast lanes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large broadband providers such as cable and telephone companies, which would face common-carrier regulation and lose the lighter-touch treatment they have operated under since 2017.

drawbacks.text: Industry opponents have long argued that common-carrier classification depresses investment in network buildout and upgrades; lighter-touch regulation was the stated rationale for the FCC's 2017 reversal of Title II rules (general knowledge applied to the classification mechanism) [S2].
Common-carrier status opens the door to broader FCC authority over pricing and service terms, which critics view as heavy-handed regulation of a competitive market [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users the protections are real and popular, but the bill's effects depend entirely on how the FCC uses its new authority rather than writing rules directly, and the industry's investment argument is a genuine, contested concern. The larger practical weakness is that the bill went nowhere, so it delivers nothing as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 28, 2022, by Rep. Doris Matsui with 29 original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
Referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed [S5].
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, and all bills not passed die at that point [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers are better off: they remain classified as lightly regulated information services and face no common-carrier or net neutrality obligations from this bill.

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to classify broadband as a telecommunications service

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — during the remainder of the Congress

against.name: Broadband industry (cable and telephone providers)
against.what_they_did: Opposed reclassification of broadband as a common-carrier service, the position the industry has consistently taken in FCC and legislative fights over Title II

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached any vote.

industries.note: Common-carrier classification would subject providers to stronger regulation, ending their ability to operate under the light-touch regime in place since 2017. Their interest in blocking reclassification runs against internet users' interest in net neutrality protections.
Net neutrality rules prevent broadband providers from charging them fees for priority delivery or degrading their traffic, so their users get equal access without extra charges.
